Big percentage days on small accounts usually mean heavy leverage, and heavy leverage means the account was close to zero on the way.
Ask for the account size, the full history and the losing days before you believe a number.

1000-dollar-day-trap.myth: A $1,000 day proves a trader can repeat it.
1000-dollar-day-trap.reality: One day is one sample. Without the account size, the leverage and every losing day, the number says nothing about the next day.

quiz.q: A post shows +$1,000 in one day on a $2,000 account. What was the return that day?
quiz.e: $1,000 / $2,000 = 0.5, so 50% in a day. Returns like that normally require leverage, which cuts both ways.

takeaways: AI is most useful as an analyst: summarising, flagging and explaining data you can check.
Giving an agent unlimited authority over funds multiplies the cost of a single mistake or a prompt-injection attack.
Hard limits belong in code (spend caps, allow-lists, human approval), not only in a prompt.

ai-meets-crypto.myth: An AI agent can trade your crypto profitably on autopilot.
ai-meets-crypto.reality: A model cannot see the future and can be tricked by text it reads. Autonomy without hard limits only makes errors bigger and faster.

quiz.q: Which is the safest first use of AI in crypto?
o: Summarising market data you then verify
Copying its price targets into orders
quiz.e: Summaries you can check keep a human in the loop. Full control and blind copying remove the check.

takeaways: Roughly every 210,000 blocks (about four years) the reward for mining a block is cut in half.
Total supply is capped at 21 million coins, and the schedule is public and fixed.
A halving changes new supply, not demand. What happened to price after past halvings is only a handful of data points.

bitcoin-halving-explained.myth: A halving makes the price go up automatically.
bitcoin-halving-explained.reality: It slows new issuance on a schedule everyone already knows. Price depends on demand and everything else that moves at the same time.

quiz.q: About how many blocks separate two Bitcoin halvings?
quiz.e: The reward halves every 210,000 blocks, which at about ten minutes a block is roughly four years.

takeaways: Fees, slippage and funding are paid on every trade, so a strategy must beat all of them before it earns anything.
Studies of active retail traders find that most lose money over time.
Two traders with the same sizing and risk-reward can land on opposite sides of zero because of a ten-point win-rate gap.

day-trading-crypto-realistic-returns.myth: If you work hard enough, daily profit is a matter of discipline.
day-trading-crypto-realistic-returns.reality: Discipline controls risk, not outcomes. Costs, small samples and luck decide a lot more than most traders expect.

quiz.q: You risk $100 per trade at a 1:2 reward and win 4 of 10 trades. What is the net result?
quiz.e: 4 wins of $200 is $800 and 6 losses of $100 is $600, so the net is +$200. At 3 wins of 10 the same plan loses $100.

takeaways: DCA is a rule about when you buy, not about what is worth buying.
It lowers the damage of a badly timed purchase and also lowers the gain from a well-timed one.
The best plan is the one small enough that you will keep running it through a drawdown.
facts: average cost of $100 at $10 then $100 at $5
simple average of the two prices, which overstates the cost

dollar-cost-averaging-crypto.reality: DCA protects you from regret about timing. If the asset keeps falling, you keep losing, just in smaller instalments.

quiz.q: You buy $100 at $10 and $100 at $5. What is your average cost per coin?
quiz.e: You hold 10 + 20 = 30 coins for $200, so the average is about $6.67. Falling prices buy more coins, which pulls the average toward the lower price.

takeaways: The index is a mood gauge built from several market inputs, not a forecast.
Extreme readings show the crowd is one-sided. They do not say when the one-sidedness ends.
Always check it against trend, funding and where price sits before acting.

fear-and-greed-index.myth: Extreme fear means it is time to buy.
fear-and-greed-index.reality: Extreme fear can last for weeks while price keeps falling. It is context that something is crowded, not a trigger.

quiz.q: The index reads 15 and price is still making new lows on rising volume. What does that most likely suggest?
o: The crowd is scared, but selling may not be over
quiz.e: Extreme fear describes sentiment. Without a pause in new lows, the selling pressure can carry on.

takeaways: Funding is a payment between traders on perpetual contracts, not a fee paid to the exchange.
It is charged on the full position size, not on your margin, so leverage makes it heavier.
A high funding rate with rising open interest points to a crowded, fragile trade.

funding-rate-explained.myth: Positive funding means the market is bullish and price must go up.
funding-rate-explained.reality: Positive funding means longs outnumber shorts. Crowded longs can be the fuel for a sharp drop just as easily as a rally.

quiz.q: Funding is positive. Who pays whom?
quiz.e: Positive funding means longs pay shorts. Negative funding reverses the direction.

takeaways: Fees apply on both entry and exit, so the break-even price is above your entry.
Several buys mean you track an average cost, not a single price.
On futures, leverage and funding change the maths, and losses are asymmetric: a 50% loss needs a 100% gain to repair.

how-to-calculate-crypto-profit-and-loss.myth: If the price is above where I bought, I am in profit.
how-to-calculate-crypto-profit-and-loss.reality: After fees (and spread, and funding on futures) the break-even is higher than your entry price. Profit starts above that line.

quiz.q: With 0.1% fee on both the buy and the sell, roughly how much must price rise to break even?
quiz.e: You pay about 0.1% going in and 0.1% going out, so price needs to rise about 0.2% before you are even.

takeaways: The book lists resting buy orders (bids) and sell orders (asks) at each price.
A market order walks up the asks (or down the bids), so your average fill is worse than the best quote. That gap is slippage.
Imbalance and big walls can change in an instant, so treat them as context, never a promise.

how-to-read-an-order-book.myth: A big wall in the order book guarantees price will stop there.
how-to-read-an-order-book.reality: Orders can be pulled at any moment. A wall is a hint of interest, and it may vanish when price gets close.

quiz.q: Asks: 2 coins at $100.00 and 3 at $100.10. You market-buy 4 coins. What is your average price?
quiz.e: 2 coins at $100.00 plus 2 at $100.10 is $400.20 for 4 coins, which is $100.05 on average.

takeaways: Impermanent loss compares your pool position with simply holding the same tokens.
It grows as the price ratio between the two tokens moves away from where you deposited.
Fees can offset it, but only the comparison against holding tells you whether you came out ahead.
facts: loss vs holding when one token doubles
loss vs holding when one token goes 4x
loss if the ratio returns to the start
impermanent-loss-explained.myth: Impermanent loss is only a paper loss, so it does not matter.
impermanent-loss-explained.reality: It is a real opportunity cost whenever you withdraw away from the original ratio. It only disappears if the ratio comes back.

quiz.q: Why is it called impermanent?
o: Because it shrinks if the price ratio returns to where it started
quiz.e: The gap versus holding is a function of the price ratio. If the ratio goes back to the deposit level, the gap closes.

quiz.e: A wider stop means more room is needed before liquidation, so safe leverage drops (about 43x at a 1% stop, about 12x at 5%).

takeaways: Open interest counts contracts that are still open, not how many traded.
Rising open interest means new positions are being added. Falling open interest means positions are being closed.
Read it with price and funding: it shows how much leverage is sitting in the market, not which way it will break.

open-interest-explained.myth: High volume and high open interest are the same thing.
open-interest-explained.reality: Volume counts every trade. Open interest only grows when new positions are opened, and falls when they are closed.

quiz.q: Alice sells her open long to Carol. What happens to open interest?
quiz.e: The same single long position still exists, only under a new owner, so open interest is unchanged while volume counted a trade.

takeaways: Size comes from the amount you are willing to lose, divided by the distance to your stop.
A wider stop means a smaller position, so the loss stays the same.
Leverage changes how much margin you post, not how much you should risk.

position-sizing-and-the-one-percent-rule.myth: If I am very confident, I should size up.
position-sizing-and-the-one-percent-rule.reality: Confidence does not change the odds on a single trade. Fixed-risk sizing keeps one wrong idea from doing outsized damage.

quiz.q: Account $5,000, risk 1%, entry $100, stop $95. How many coins?
quiz.e: Risk is $50 and the stop distance is $5 per coin, so $50 / $5 = 10 coins.

Expectancy combines win rate and reward size, which is why a 40% win rate can still make money.
Losing streaks are a normal part of any edge, so judge a strategy only over a large sample.

risk-reward-ratio-and-win-rate.myth: A high win rate means a good strategy.
risk-reward-ratio-and-win-rate.reality: Many small wins can be erased by a few large losses. Win rate only means something together with the average win and loss.

quiz.q: What is the break-even win rate when you target 2R and risk 1R?
quiz.e: At 1:2, break-even is 1 / (1 + 2) = 33.3%, before fees.

takeaways: Round numbers matter because orders cluster there, not because the digits are special.
Whether a level holds depends on how many resting orders are there versus how much buying or selling arrives.
Confirm with the order book, volume and timeframe before treating it as support or resistance.

round-number-levels.reality: Levels get absorbed all the time. If buyers run out, price goes through and the cluster is gone.

quiz.q: Why do round numbers sometimes act as support or resistance?
quiz.e: Clustered orders around a salient price create real supply and demand at that level.

takeaways: Spot means you own the coin. Perpetual futures mean you hold a leveraged contract on its price.
With leverage, a move against you can liquidate the position well before the price reaches zero.
Perpetuals add funding payments, which spot does not have.

spot-vs-futures.myth: Futures are just spot with a bigger payout.
spot-vs-futures.reality: Futures add liquidation, funding and the risk of losing everything you posted, which spot does not.

quiz.q: You hold a 10x long and price falls about 10%. What most likely happens?
quiz.e: 10x leverage means a 10% adverse move consumes the margin. Exchanges also require maintenance margin, so liquidation happens slightly sooner.

takeaways: A stop-market order is nearly guaranteed to execute but may fill beyond your price.
A stop-limit order guarantees a worst price but may not fill at all.
On futures, make sure your stop is hit before your liquidation price, with room to spare.

stop-loss-orders-explained.myth: A stop-loss guarantees the maximum loss I set.
stop-loss-orders-explained.reality: In fast markets a stop-market can fill worse, and a stop-limit can fail to fill. A stop controls intent, not the exact price.

quiz.q: Which order type can leave you still holding the position after a fast drop through your price?
quiz.e: If price passes your limit before it can fill, a stop-limit may sit unfilled while the loss grows.

takeaways: Price reflects the combined decisions of millions of participants, so confident point forecasts are rarely trustworthy.
Write if/then plans before a trade: what must hold, and what proves the idea wrong.
Check positioning, levels and context instead of chasing a target.

why-we-dont-predict-crypto-prices.myth: Better AI will eventually predict prices reliably.
why-we-dont-predict-crypto-prices.reality: Better models can describe conditions faster, but the future still depends on events and behaviour that are not in the data yet.

quiz.q: What should you write down before a trade instead of a price target?
